question: What is the industry standard supply for constant-frequency aircraft?

options.text: 28 V DC with 115 V single-phase standby
115 V / 200 V, 60 Hz, single phase only

explanation: Large aircraft use 115 V phase, 200 V line, 400 Hz three-phase AC. DC is obtained from it with TRUs.

question: How is 28 V DC obtained in a large AC aircraft?

options.text: From static inverters fed by AC
From the AC supply through TRUs
From the APU's DC output only
From separate DC generators on each engine

explanation: Transformer rectifier units convert AC to 28 V DC; the battery is kept for emergency use.

question: What is emphasised in the layout of an AC bus bar system?

options.text: Using as few bus bars as possible to save weight
Feeding all loads from the battery
Coping with failure with least loss of service

explanation: As in DC systems, the buses form a hierarchy designed to cope with failure with the least possible loss of electrical services.

question: What is another name for an AC generator?
explanation: An AC generator is called an alternator.

question: Which part rotates in a DC generator, and is it always so in an AC generator?

options.text: The field; never in an alternator of any size
The armature; usually not in an alternator
The armature; always in an alternator too
The field; always in an alternator too

explanation: A DC generator always has a rotating armature. Most alternators instead rotate the field and keep the armature stationary.

question: Where is a rotating armature alternator used?

options.text: In all large aircraft AC systems

explanation: The rotating armature type takes its AC output through slip rings and is used only for very small outputs, not for supplying aircraft AC systems.

question: How is the output taken from a rotating armature alternator?
explanation: The AC induced in the rotating armature is taken out as AC through slip rings, not commutated to DC.

question: In most practical alternators, what does the rotor carry?
explanation: Most alternators have a rotating field (rotor) and a stationary armature (stator).

question: How may the rotating field of an alternator be energised?

options.text: By AC taken from its own stator windings
By a permanent magnet or by DC

explanation: The field is energised by a permanent magnet or by DC from a separate source. It must be DC so the rotor poles keep their polarity.

question: Why must an alternator's rotating field be fed with DC rather than AC?

options.text: To keep the output frequency at zero
To keep the rotor poles' polarity

explanation: Only DC keeps each rotor pole a fixed north or south; AC would make the poles keep reversing.

question: What is an advantage of a rotating field alternator?

options.text: Only low field current passes through the slip rings
It needs no excitation at all
The full output current passes through the slip rings

explanation: Only the small field current goes through the slip rings; the heavy output comes from the stationary armature, so brush arcing is greatly reduced.

question: What limits the maximum output current of an alternator?

options.text: The heat its armature can sustain
The size of its slip rings

explanation: Current heats the armature conductors and, in extreme cases, destroys the winding insulation. The heat that can be sustained sets the limit.

question: In what units are alternators rated?
explanation: Alternators are rated by armature current and voltage, so in volt-amperes or kilovolt-amperes — apparent power.

question: How are the stator windings of a single-phase alternator connected?

options.text: In parallel, opposing each other, to cancel ripple

explanation: The windings are series-aiding so that their induced voltages add in phase. The rotor has two poles of opposite polarity.

question: What decides the number of phases of an alternator?
explanation: A polyphase alternator has two or more single-phase windings spaced around the stator; each separate winding gives one phase.

question: How do the outputs of a polyphase alternator compare?

options.text: Same frequency, equally out of phase
Different frequencies and phases for each winding

explanation: All phases have the same frequency, but corresponding values are separated by an equal number of degrees.

question: By how much are the phases of a three-phase alternator separated?
explanation: The three windings are mechanically 120° apart, so the outputs are electrically 120° apart.

question: What is meant by phase sequence ABC?

options.text: C peaks first, then B, then A
A peaks first, then B, then C
A and C peak together, with B 180° later

explanation: The phases reach their positive peaks in the order A, then B, then C.

question: Which is an advantage of a three-phase system?

options.text: It works without a neutral at all times

explanation: Three-phase systems have a better power-to-weight ratio and are easier to connect in parallel.

question: What are the two ways of connecting a three-phase alternator?
explanation: The three phases are connected either in star (with a neutral) or in delta (a closed mesh).

question: In a star-connected alternator, what is the neutral point?

options.text: The free end of each phase
The point where line voltage is measured
The point joining one end of each phase

explanation: One end of each phase is joined to form a fourth connection, the neutral, normally grounded as the earth return.

question: What does the neutral line of a star system carry?

options.text: The full current of all three phases at all times
Only DC current from the TRUs

explanation: With balanced loads the neutral carries little; any imbalance flows in it. An earth fault on one phase gives the neutral a very high load.

question: Why is a star-connected alternator used for aircraft distribution?

options.text: It has equal line and phase voltage
It copes with unequal phase loads

explanation: The neutral lets the star system handle different loads on each phase bus; the delta connection cannot.

question: In a star system, phase voltage is measured between:
explanation: Line to neutral is phase voltage; line to line is line voltage.

question: In a star system, how is line voltage related to phase voltage?
explanation: Line voltage is the vector sum of two phases 120° apart: √3 × phase, about 1.73 × phase.

question: A star system has a phase voltage of 115 V. What is the line voltage?
explanation: 115 × 1.73 ≈ 199 V, quoted as 200 V. Dividing by 1.73 gives 66 V; simply doubling gives 230 V.

question: A star system has a line voltage of 208 V. What is the phase voltage?
explanation: Phase = 208 ÷ 1.73 ≈ 120 V. Halving gives 104 V; multiplying gives 360 V.

question: In a star connection, how does line current compare with phase current?

options.text: Line current is half phase current

explanation: Each line is in series with its phase winding, so in star the line current equals the phase current.

question: How are the phases of a delta-connected alternator joined?

options.text: End to end in a closed mesh

explanation: In delta the ends of the phases are joined to form a closed loop, with the loads connected the same way.

question: In a delta connection, how does line voltage compare with phase voltage?
explanation: In delta each phase winding sits directly between two lines, so line voltage equals phase voltage.

question: In a delta connection, how is line current related to phase current?
explanation: Each line joins two phase windings, so line current is the vector sum: √3 (1.73) times the phase current.

question: A delta alternator has a phase current of 10 A. What is the line current?
explanation: Line current = 1.73 × 10 = 17.3 A. Dividing gives 5.8 A and tripling gives 30 A.

question: Why is delta connection not used for aircraft distribution?

options.text: Without a neutral it can't handle unbalance
Its line voltage is too low

explanation: Without a neutral the delta cannot handle unequal phase loads, so it is used only for special purposes such as speed sensors and tacho generators.

question: Which is a disadvantage of a rotating armature alternator?

options.text: Its rotating coils are hard to cool
It gives too high a power-to-weight ratio
It has no slip rings at all
Its field current passes through the brushes

explanation: Rotating coils are heavy with high centrifugal forces, hard to insulate and cool, brush resistance is high, and the power-to-weight ratio is poor.

question: What are the two types of rotating field alternator used on aircraft?
explanation: Rotating field alternators are either brushed, with slip rings feeding the field, or brushless, with an exciter and rotating rectifier.

question: In a brushed alternator, how does excitation current reach the rotor field?

options.text: From a permanent magnet generator only

explanation: DC, at first from the battery and then from rectified AC, is fed through brushes and slip rings to the rotating field.

question: What does the voltage regulator of a brushed alternator sample?
explanation: It samples the AC output and adjusts the excitation current to hold the voltage whatever the speed and load.

question: What does a brushless alternator use instead of brushes to feed its main field?

options.text: A battery mounted on the rotor

explanation: An exciter generator on the same shaft produces AC, which a rotating rectifier turns to DC for the main rotor field.

question: What does the rotating rectifier in a brushless alternator do?

options.text: Turns exciter AC into DC for the field
Converts DC to AC for the exciter
Converts the main output to DC for the bus

explanation: It turns the AC from the exciter armature into the DC the main rotor field needs.

question: How is the output voltage of a brushless alternator regulated?

options.text: By varying the main stator turns

explanation: Controlling the exciter field controls the exciter output, the main field current and so the alternator voltage.

question: Which is an advantage of a brushless alternator?
explanation: Brushless alternators are very reliable, have no brush wear and a high power-to-weight ratio.

question: What does the permanent magnet generator (PMG) in a modern brushless alternator supply?
explanation: A PMG on the same shaft provides excitation current for the exciter, giving three generators on one shaft.

question: What are the two basic types of brushless alternator?
explanation: An externally excited type has no residual magnetism in its exciter; a self-excited type has some.

question: What is a frequency wild alternator?

options.text: One whose frequency is held at 400 Hz
One whose frequency follows engine speed

explanation: Driven straight from the engine gearbox, its speed and frequency vary directly with engine speed.

question: Can two frequency wild alternators be paralleled?
explanation: Their frequencies vary independently with engine speed, so they cannot be connected in parallel.

question: What are frequency wild supplies typically used for?
explanation: Heater mats are resistive, so their behaviour is not affected by frequency changes, which suits a frequency wild supply.

question: How can a constant-frequency supply be obtained from a frequency wild alternator?

options.text: Connect it in parallel with a second alternator
Rectify it to DC, then use a static inverter
Pass it through a capacitor bank

explanation: Wild AC is rectified to DC, which powers a static inverter producing constant-frequency AC.

question: How is a constant output frequency normally obtained?

options.text: By running the engine at constant speed
By adding more rotor poles in flight
By a capacitor bank on the output
By driving it at constant speed

explanation: Frequency depends on speed, and running the engine at constant speed is impractical, so a drive unit holds alternator speed constant.

question: What does a constant speed drive unit (CSDU) consist of?

options.text: An electric motor driving a generator
A gearbox with fixed ratios only
A hydraulic pump driving a hydraulic motor

explanation: The engine drives a hydraulic pump whose output drives a hydraulic motor, which drives the alternator at constant speed.

question: Where does a CSDU get its oil?
explanation: The CSDU's oil, which also lubricates and cools it, is in a reservoir entirely separate from the engine oil.

question: What sets the output speed of a CSDU's hydraulic pump?

options.text: The angle of a swash plate
The number of pump pistons removed

explanation: The swash plate angle decides pump output and so hydraulic motor speed. A speed governor sets the angle.

question: What senses the alternator frequency and controls the CSDU torque?
explanation: The load controller senses output frequency and, through the governor and swash plate, raises or lowers the CSDU's torque output.

question: Within what limits do most CSDUs hold frequency?
explanation: Most CSDUs maintain the output within about 5% of 400 Hz, that is 380–420 Hz.

question: What protects a CSDU if its alternator suffers a mechanical failure?

options.text: A fuse in the field circuit

explanation: The quill drive is a weak link that breaks before major damage can be done.

question: In which CSDU mode is the engine slower than the generator?
explanation: Overdrive: engine speed is less than generator speed. Underdrive: engine faster than generator. Straight-through: the same.

question: In which CSDU mode is the engine faster than the generator?
explanation: In underdrive the drive reduces the speed, so the engine turns faster than the generator.

question: What is an IDG?

options.text: An inverter driven by a gas turbine
An inertial drive governor for the engine
A CSDU and generator in one unit

explanation: An Integrated Drive Generator (or IDU) combines the constant speed drive and the generator in one unit.

question: Which two warnings are associated with a CSDU in the cockpit?

options.text: Low voltage and high frequency on the bus
Low oil pressure, high oil temperature
Low fuel pressure and high EGT

explanation: Low oil pressure lights and high oil temperature indication are the main CSDU fault indications.

question: What does operating the drive disconnect do?

options.text: Disconnects the alternator from its bus only
Separates the drive from the engine

explanation: The dog clutch separates the engine input, letting the drive and alternator come to rest so the fault cannot affect the engine.

question: When can a disconnected generator drive be reconnected?

options.text: Only on the ground, engine stopped
At any time in flight by the pilot

explanation: Disconnection can be done any time the engine runs, but reconnection is manual, on the ground, after engine shutdown.

question: What kind of switch is the drive disconnect switch?
explanation: The momentary-action switch operates a solenoid that separates the drive. It is guarded to prevent inadvertent use.

question: Can a generator drive ever disconnect automatically?

options.text: Yes, on every aircraft, whenever frequency drops
On some aircraft, via the GCU
Only when the pilot holds the switch

explanation: Exceptionally, some aircraft let the generator control unit disconnect the drive automatically under certain fault conditions.

question: How does a VSCF system produce a constant frequency?

options.text: Using a hydromechanical constant speed drive
Running the engine at constant speed
Using a frequency wild supply directly

explanation: A frequency wild generator's output is rectified, filtered and inverted by a generator converter control unit to 115/200 V, 400 Hz, three phase.

question: What does a VSCF system eliminate?
explanation: Electronic conversion removes the need for the CSDU and its controls, improving reliability.

question: Why is a VSCF system flexible to install?

options.text: It works only on the ground with external power
Its converter can be sited away from the engine

explanation: The electronic converter can be placed away from the generator, outside the engine compartment.

question: What is a self-excited brushless generator?

options.text: One that needs the battery for its field
One with no exciter at all
One fed with AC to its rotor field
One with residual magnetism in its exciter

explanation: Stationary permanent magnets in the exciter induce AC in its rotor on first rotation, which the rotating rectifier feeds as DC to the main field.

question: In a self-excited generator, what then supplies the exciter field once running?

options.text: A supply tapped from the main output
The PMG only, permanently, at a fixed level

explanation: The main stator output is tapped to give a regulated supply to the exciter field, so the voltage can be controlled.

question: Which two quantities must be shared between paralleled constant-frequency alternators?
explanation: Load sharing requires control of both real load (kW) and reactive load (kVAR).

question: What is real load measured in?
explanation: Real load is the working output available for services, measured in kW (true power).

question: Real load is directly related to:
explanation: Real load corresponds to the mechanical power or torque fed to the alternator by the engine or CSDU.

question: How is real load sharing achieved?

options.text: By opening the bus tie breakers in turn

explanation: Adjusting each CSDU's torque so that all are equal makes each generator take the same real load.

question: What is reactive load measured in?
explanation: Reactive (wattless) load is measured in kilovolt-amperes reactive.

question: How is reactive load sharing achieved?
explanation: Reactive load is shared by controlling each generator's exciter field current so their voltages are identical.

question: When is a generator connected into the load sharing circuits?
explanation: A generator running on its own, as at engine start, is not connected to the load sharing circuits.

question: Why must alternators be at the same frequency before paralleling?

options.text: Otherwise the neutral current falls to zero
One would be forced to slow, the other to speed up

explanation: Alternators are synchronous machines that lock together in parallel. Joining them at different frequencies forces one to slow and the other to accelerate, which can cause damage.

question: Which conditions must be met before alternators are paralleled?

options.text: Same load, oil temperature and running hours

explanation: Frequency, voltage and phase sequence must all match within strict limits.

question: What connects a generator to its own bus in a paralleled system?

options.text: A reverse current cut-out relay on each phase

explanation: Each generator feeds its own three-phase bus through a three-phase GCB, controlled automatically or from the flight deck.

question: What connects each generator bus to the synchronising bus?
explanation: BTBs link the generator buses to the synchronising bus so the generators can run in parallel.

question: What loads does the synchronising bus carry?
explanation: The synchronising bus carries no loads; it exists only to allow the generators to be paralleled.

question: On the ground with engine generators off, how can ground power reach the load buses?

options.text: It cannot reach the load buses
Via the synchronising bus and BTBs

explanation: Ground power or the APU generator can feed the synchronising bus and from there the load buses through the BTBs, with the GCBs open.

subtopic: Real and reactive load sharing circuits
question: What senses the real load distribution between paralleled alternators?

options.text: Frequency meters on each generator output

explanation: Current transformers in a series loop sense each alternator's load; error detectors across them detect imbalance.

subtopic: Real and reactive load sharing circuits
question: Three paralleled alternators share load equally with 5 A in each current transformer. What flows in the error detectors?
explanation: With balanced load every transformer matches the average, so no current is pushed through the error detectors.

subtopic: Real and reactive load sharing circuits
question: No. 1 alternator's CT current rises to 7 A and the others fall to 4 A. What does the load sharing circuit do?

options.text: Cuts No. 1 torque, raises Nos. 2 and 3

explanation: The differences from the 5 A average drive the error detectors; the speed governors cut No. 1's torque and raise the others' until loads balance again.

subtopic: Real and reactive load sharing circuits
question: What does the mutual reactor in a reactive load sharing circuit do?

options.text: Converts reactive load into real load
Measures the frequency of each generator
Isolates the reactive part of the current

explanation: The mutual reactor is a phase-shifting transformer so the error detector responds only to reactive current.

subtopic: Real and reactive load sharing circuits
question: Where are the correcting signals of the reactive load sharing circuit sent?
explanation: Reactive imbalance is corrected by raising the voltage of the low generator and lowering the high one through their field circuits.

subtopic: Real and reactive load sharing circuits
question: How do most modern twin-engine aircraft run their two generators?

options.text: With one permanently on standby and unloaded

explanation: Three- and four-generator aircraft typically parallel them, but most twins run their generators separately on a split bus.

question: How are frequency wild generators and those with separate CSDUs typically cooled?

options.text: Ram air, with induced airflow on the ground

explanation: These typically use ram air in flight and some means of inducing airflow on the ground.

question: How is an IDG's stator cooled?
explanation: IDGs use their own oil to cool the stator; the oil is cooled in the IDG's own oil cooler.

question: What is the position of the BTBs in a paralleled system?

options.text: Open in flight, closed on the ground

explanation: In a paralleled system the BTBs are normally closed. In a split bus system they are normally open.

question: What must a BTB receive before it closes to parallel an alternator?

options.text: A signal from the battery charger
A manual reset from the engineer

explanation: The synchronising unit checks phase, frequency and voltage; only then may the BTB close.

question: What do discriminatory circuits ensure?

options.text: Only the faulty part is disconnected
All generators are disconnected after a fault
The fault is ignored until after landing
The battery supplies all loads after a fault

explanation: By selective switching of GCBs and BTBs, discrimination isolates only the faulty system from its bus.

question: What does a bus power control unit (BPCU) do?

options.text: Isolates faults and reconfigures the system

explanation: Using current transformers at each generator and bus, the BPCU isolates a defective generator or bus and reconfigures for maximum use.

question: Which is a differential current fault?

options.text: An open bus tie breaker in a split bus
A short between buses or to ground

explanation: Differential protection detects shorts between buses or to ground, and open circuits unbalancing the phases.

question: Which conditions are protected against in an AC generating system?
explanation: Protection covers over/under voltage, over/under frequency, over/under excitation and differential current faults.

question: What two synchronising methods are in use?
explanation: Automatic control checks voltage, frequency and phase sequence before closing the breaker; the older dark lamp method relies on the crew.

question: In the dark lamp method, when may the breaker be closed?

options.text: When the synchronising lamps are dark
When one lamp is lit and the other dark

explanation: The lamps show differences between the two supplies; when they are dark the supplies are in synchronism and the breaker can be closed.

question: When does a generator failure warning light illuminate?

options.text: When its CSDU oil is cold

explanation: The light comes on when its GCB trips, together with the central warning system and, on some aircraft, an aural warning.

question: What do kW/kVAR meters show in a paralleled system?

options.text: kW or kVAR, by a selector

explanation: One meter can show kW or kVAR; it normally shows kW, with kVAR selected by a switch or button.

question: What is the reactive load used for in the circuits?

options.text: Doing useful work at the bus

explanation: Reactive (wattless) load creates the magnetic and electric fields in the circuits. Real load is what does work.

question: How many voltmeters and frequency meters are usually fitted with several alternators?

options.text: None; only load meters are fitted
One of each, with a selector

explanation: Typically one voltmeter and one frequency meter are fitted, with a multi-position switch to select any source, including APU, ground power and RAT.

question: What does a generator control unit (GCU) do?

options.text: Controls the CSDU oil temperature only

explanation: The GCU regulates voltage by controlling exciter field current and protects against overvoltage, overcurrent, frequency, phase sequence and differential faults.

question: In a dangerous fault such as overvoltage, what does the GCU do?

options.text: Opens the exciter relay and the GCB
Closes the BTB to share the fault

explanation: Opening the exciter (generator field) relay drops output to residual, and opening the GCB disconnects the generator from its bus.

question: After a GCU trips a generator in a paralleled system, how is its bus kept powered?

options.text: By the others through the BTB

explanation: In a paralleled system the other generators keep supplying the generator bus through the bus tie breaker.

question: Which is an emergency source of AC?
explanation: Alternative AC sources include the RAT, the APU, a static inverter and a hydraulic-motor-driven generator.

question: What does an electrical RAT supply after total generator failure?
explanation: The RAT gives a nominal 115/200 V, 400 Hz, three-phase supply for limited operation of flight instruments and radio.

question: What is an APU?

options.text: A small gas turbine in the tail cone
A battery pack in the cargo hold
A diesel generator on the ground
A wind turbine on the wing

explanation: The APU is usually a small constant-speed gas turbine in the tail cone, with its own fire, oil, overspeed and overheat protection.

question: Can the APU generator be paralleled with the engine generators?

options.text: No; only when nothing else feeds the bus

explanation: The APU alternator cannot be paralleled with the engine generators and supplies the buses only when nothing else is feeding them.

question: Why does the APU generator need no constant speed drive?

options.text: The APU generator is frequency wild
The APU drives a static inverter
The APU runs at a constant speed

explanation: The APU itself runs at constant speed, so its generator gives constant frequency without a CSDU.

question: What powers the emergency static inverter?

options.text: The batteries or essential DC bus
Ground power only, through the external socket

explanation: The static inverter is fed from the batteries or an essential DC bus and supplies AC for limited instrument and radio services.

question: What is the standard output of a modern ground power unit?
explanation: Standard GPU output matches the aircraft supply: 115/200 V, 400 Hz, three phase, able to supply all services.

question: Which protection must ground power have?

options.text: It must be paralleled with the engine generators
It must accept any voltage it is supplied
It cannot connect if the phase sequence is wrong
It must connect even if the aircraft generators are on line

explanation: Ground power cannot connect while the aircraft's own alternators supply the system, cannot connect with the wrong phase sequence, and is rejected on overvoltage.

question: On a typical AC panel, what does the generator field "trip" switch light do?
explanation: The field switch lights control the exciter control relay; "trip" opens the field so generator voltage falls to zero.

question: What does each AC bus feed in a typical three-engine system?

options.text: A RAT supplying the essential bus
A static inverter supplying the hot bus
A TRU supplying its DC bus

explanation: Each AC bus feeds a TRU that converts 115/200 V AC to 28 V DC for its DC bus; the DC buses are normally tied.

question: What do the red fail lights on the essential and standby buses indicate?

options.text: The bus tie breakers are closed
The buses are fed from the battery

explanation: The red fail lights show that there is no voltage on the essential or standby bus bars.
